claim: Postsynaptic spike firing elicited fast mitochondrial Ca2+ responses that were about threefold larger in the somas and apical dendrites than in basal dendrites and axons.
source: Postsynaptic spike firing elicited fast mitochondrial Ca2+ responses that were about threefold larger in the somas and apical dendrites than in basal dendrites and axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential mitochondrial Ca2+ responses across neuronal compartments, as presented in Figure 1d-e.

claim: The amplitude of mitochondrial Ca2+ responses and metabolic activity were extremely sensitive to the firing frequency.
source: The amplitude of these responses and metabolic activity were extremely sensitive to the firing frequency.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing frequency-dependent changes in mitochondrial Ca2+ signals and NAD(P)H metabolism, as shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: While an EPSP alone caused no detectable Ca2+ elevation in the dendritic mitochondria, the coincidence of EPSP with a backpropagating spike produced prominent, highly localized mitochondrial Ca2+ hotspots.
source: Furthermore, while an EPSP alone caused no detectable Ca2+ elevation in the dendritic mitochondria, the coincidence of EPSP with a backpropagating spike produced prominent, highly localized mitochondrial Ca2+ hotspots.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing that paired EPSP and AP stimulation produces localized mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations, as demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: Mitochondria decode the spike firing frequency and the Hebbian temporal coincidences into Ca2+ signals, which are further translated into the metabolic output.
source: Our results indicate that mitochondria decode the spike firing frequency and the Hebbian temporal coincidences into the Ca2+ signals, which are further translated into the metabolic output and most probably lead to long-term changes in synaptic efficacy.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing frequency-dependent mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling and metabolic changes, as well as spike-timing-dependent mitochondrial responses.

claim: Mitochondrial activity is crucial for the plasticity of central synapses.
source: Mitochondrial activity is crucial for the plasticity of central synapses, but how the firing pattern of pre- and postsynaptic neurons affects the mitochondria remains elusive.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial roles in synaptic plasticity.

claim: When cytosolic [Ca2+]i rises, Ca2+ ions, powered by the steep mitochondrial membrane potential, flow into the mitochondrial matrix via the Ca2+ uniporter MCU.
source: When cytosolic [Ca2+]i rises, Ca2+ ions, powered by the steep mitochondrial membrane potential, flow into the mitochondrial matrix via the Ca2+ uniporter MCU (Baughman et al., 2011; De Stefani et al., 2011), and are then extruded back into the cytosol by the mitochondrial Na+/Ca2+ antiporter NCLX (Palty et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake mechanisms.

claim: Ca2+ ions are extruded back into the cytosol from mitochondria by the mitochondrial Na+/Ca2+ antiporter NCLX.
source: When cytosolic [Ca2+]i rises, Ca2+ ions, powered by the steep mitochondrial membrane potential, flow into the mitochondrial matrix via the Ca2+ uniporter MCU (Baughman et al., 2011; De Stefani et al., 2011), and are then extruded back into the cytosol by the mitochondrial Na+/Ca2+ antiporter NCLX (Palty et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research on mitochondrial Ca2+ extrusion mechanisms.

claim: The mitochondrial Ca2+ elevation increases ATP production by activating at least three Krebs cycle enzymes.
source: The mitochondrial Ca2+ elevation increases ATP production by activating at least three Krebs cycle enzymes (De Stefani et al., 2016; Wescott et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on Ca2+-dependent activation of Krebs cycle enzymes.

claim: When Ca2+ signaling is disrupted, mitochondria in presynaptic terminals fail to maintain the stable ATP concentration during enhanced activity periods.
source: When Ca2+ signaling is disrupted, mitochondria in presynaptic terminals fail to maintain the stable ATP concentration during enhanced activity periods (Ashrafi et al., 2020; Giorgio et al., 2013; Glancy and Balaban, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on the role of Ca2+ signaling in mitochondrial ATP production.

claim: Dendritic mitochondria play a critical role in long-term regulation of synaptic strength.
source: Recent evidence using photo-uncaging of glutamate on spines of cultured hippocampal neurons indicates that dendritic mitochondria play a critical role in long-term regulation of synaptic strength (Rangaraju et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research on dendritic mitochondria and synaptic plasticity.

claim: Local inhibition of the mitochondria by a phototoxic protein abolishes the synaptic plasticity in the affected dendritic segment.
source: Thus, local inhibition of the mitochondria by a phototoxic protein abolishes the synaptic plasticity in the affected dendritic segment.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from cited research on mitochondrial inhibition and synaptic plasticity.

claim: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) relies on activation of the postsynaptic NMDA receptors, which are Ca2+ permeable and require both glutamate and depolarization to open.
source: Spike-timing–dependent plasticity (STDP) relies on activation of the postsynaptic NMDA receptors, which are Ca2+ permeable and require both glutamate and depolarization to open (Nowak et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research on NMDA receptor properties and their role in STDP.

claim: Mitochondrial handling of Ca2+ ions has a significant effect on cytosolic Ca2+ dynamics.
source: Mitochondrial handling of Ca2+ ions is known to have a significant effect on cytosolic Ca2+ dynamics (Rizzuto et al., 2004; Szabadkai and Duchen, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on mitochondrial Ca2+ handling.

claim: Mitochondrial depletion had no effect on glutamate evoked cytosolic Ca2+ dynamics.
source: The mitochondrial depletion, however, had no effect on glutamate evoked cytosolic Ca2+ dynamics (Rangaraju et al., 2019), indicating that these organelles play a yet unexplored downstream role in the cascade of reactions leading to STDP.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research on mitochondrial depletion effects.

claim: Single or few spikes trigger rapidly rising and decaying mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations in all neuronal compartments, with kinetics similar to cytosolic Ca2+ transients.
source: Here, using whole-cell electrical recordings from Layer 5 pyramidal neurons in cortical slices and fluorescence imaging of cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ indicators, we show that single or few spikes trigger rapidly rising and decaying mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations in all neuronal compartments, with kinetics similar to cytosolic Ca2+ transients.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings and Ca2+ imaging.

claim: The mitochondria's Ca2+ signaling and metabolic rate depend critically on spike firing frequency.
source: Our evidence indicates that the mitochondria's Ca2+ signaling and metabolic rate depend critically on spike firing frequency.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing frequency-dependent effects on mitochondrial Ca2+ and metabolism.

claim: In dendrites, the coincidence of unitary EPSP and a backpropagating action potential produces a localized [Ca2+]m transient.
source: We further report that, in dendrites, the coincidence of unitary EPSP and a backpropagating action potential produces a localized [Ca2+]m transient, which, in addition to enhancing local ATP synthesis, could play a role in STDP.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing localized mitochondrial Ca2+ responses to paired stimulation.

claim: Two APs elicited by the injection of two brief current pulses via the patch pipette caused cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations in the soma of an L5 cell.
source: In a typical experiment, two APs elicited by the injection of two brief current pulses via the patch pipette caused cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations in the soma of an L5 cell (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The cytosolic Ca2+ signals had relatively even intensity, while the change in mitoGCaMP6m fluorescence occurred at 'hotspots', each representing an individual mitochondrion.
source: Although the cytosolic Ca2+ signals had relatively even intensity, the change in mitoGCaMP6m fluorescence occurred at 'hotspots', each representing an individual mitochondrion.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from fluorescence imaging.

claim: The mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations began with a short delay after the beginning of the spike train.
source: The mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations began with a short delay after the beginning of the spike train, and they were observed only in the electrically active neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from fluorescence imaging.

claim: Mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations were observed only in the electrically active neurons.
source: The mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations began with a short delay after the beginning of the spike train, and they were observed only in the electrically active neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations comparing active and inactive neurons, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fluorescence of nearby mitoGCaMP6m expressing mitochondria belonging to non-active cells did not change.
source: At the same time, the fluorescence of the nearby mitoGCaMP6m expressing mitochondria belonging to the non-active cells did not change (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bath application of Cd2+ (200 µM) inhibited both cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ transients.
source: It is likely that Ca2+ ions enter via the voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, as bath application of Cd2+ (200 µM) inhibited both cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ transients (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ca2+ ions enter mitochondria via the voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: It is likely that Ca2+ ions enter via the voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, as bath application of Cd2+ (200 µM) inhibited both cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ transients (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the effect of Cd2+ blockade on Ca2+ transients.

claim: Ca2+ depletion of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in cultured neurons does not influence mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations.
source: Previous studies have shown that Ca2+ depletion of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in cultured neurons does not influence mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations (Ashrafi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Blockade of ER Ca2+ channels by Ryanodine (100 µM) and Dantrolene (100 µM) had no significant effect on mitochondrial Ca2+ transients.
source: Consistent with these results, we found that blockade of ER Ca2+ channels by Ryanodine (100 µM) and Dantrolene (100 µM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) had no significant effect on mitochondrial Ca2+ transients.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: An increase in the number of spikes produced progressively larger mitoGCaMP6m transients in the soma.
source: An increase in the number of spikes produced progressively larger mitoGCaMP6m transients in the soma (Figure 1b) and the apical dendrite (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) with a progressively slower rising phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: An increase in the number of spikes produced progressively larger mitoGCaMP6m transients in the apical dendrite with a progressively slower rising phase.
source: An increase in the number of spikes produced progressively larger mitoGCaMP6m transients in the soma (Figure 1b) and the apical dendrite (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) with a progressively slower rising phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The mito-Ca2+ signals elicited by 50 APs reached a peak ΔF/F value of 59% ± 11% (n = 29) for soma and 54% ± 11% (n = 22) for apical dendrite at 120 ± 18ms (n = 10) after the train end.
source: Thus, the mito-Ca2+ signals elicited by 50 APs grew throughout the spike train duration, reaching a peak ΔF/F value of 59% ± 11% (n = 29) and 54% ± 11% (n = 22) for soma and apical dendrite, respectively, at 120 ± 18ms (n = 10) after the train end.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data.

claim: Mito-Ca2+ transients elicited by 2–20 spikes decayed as rapidly or even faster than cytosolic Ca2+ transients.
source: In contrast with previous reports (Ashrafi et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2019), mito-Ca2+ transients elicited by 2–20 spikes decayed as rapidly or even faster than cytosolic Ca2+ transients.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and contrasts with previous reports.

claim: Following large elevations, [Ca2+]m remained high for tens of seconds, reaching the resting level long after the cytosolic Ca2+ concentration completely recovered.
source: However, following large elevations, [Ca2+]m remained high for tens of seconds, reaching the resting level long after the cytosolic Ca2+ concentration completely recovered.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of Ca2+ dynamics.

claim: Decay of smaller transients (peak ΔF/F < 40%) was always monoexponential, with τ = 0.86 ± 0.11 s (n = 25).
source: Decay of smaller transients (peak ΔF/F < 40%) was always monoexponential, with τ = 0.86 ± 0.11 s (n = 25) as well as decay of some middle-sized (ΔF/F 40–75%) transients (τ = 0.82 ± 0.10 s, n = 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of decay kinetics from 42 neurons, as shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The decay of middle size and large (ΔF/F > 75%) transients was double exponential, with τ1 = 0.86 ± 0.13 s and τ2 = 22.0 ± 2.85 s (n = 23).
source: The decay of other middle size and large (ΔF/F > 75%) transients was double exponential, with τ1 = 0.86 ± 0.13 s and τ2 = 22.0 ± 2.85 s (n = 23).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of decay kinetics.

claim: The decay of cytosolic Ca2+ transients always followed a single exponential time course which was characterized by τ = 1.03 ± 0.14 s (n = 22) for small and τ = 1.19 ± 0.4 s (n = 20, p = 0.43) for large transients.
source: The decay of cytosolic Ca2+ transients always followed a single exponential time course which was characterized by τ = 1.03 ± 0.14 s (n = 22) for small and τ = 1.19 ± 0.4 s (n = 20, p = 0.43) for large transients.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cytosolic Ca2+ decay kinetics.

claim: The amplitude of the cytosolic Ca2+ responses in soma, apical dendrites, basal dendrites, and axon initial segments were similar.
source: While the amplitude and time course of the cytosolic Ca2+ responses in all these compartments were similar, the magnitude of mitochondrial signals was remarkably polar.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations comparing different neuronal compartments.

claim: The magnitude of mitochondrial signals was remarkably polar across different neuronal compartments.
source: While the amplitude and time course of the cytosolic Ca2+ responses in all these compartments were similar, the magnitude of mitochondrial signals was remarkably polar.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The amplitude of the mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations in apical dendrite was as prominent as in the soma.
source: The amplitude of the mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations in apical dendrite was as prominent as in the soma.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing mitochondrial Ca2+ responses in different compartments.

claim: In the AIS and thin basal dendrites, the mito-Ca2+ responses were dramatically smaller than in soma and apical dendrites.
source: In contrast, in the AIS and thin basal dendrites, the mito-Ca2+ responses were dramatically smaller.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d-e.

claim: The steepness of the relationship between the number of APs and the mean peak amplitude of the mitoGCaMP6m transients was greater in soma and apical dendrites (1.3% and 1.1% ΔF/F per spike, respectively) compared with AIS and basal dendrites (0.4% and 0.3% ΔF/F per spike, respectively).
source: The steepness of this relationship was greater in soma and apical dendrites (1.3% and 1.1% ΔF/F per spike, respectively) compared with AIS and basal dendrites (0.4% and 0.3% ΔF/F per spike, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of data from 29 neurons, as shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The compartmental differences in mitochondrial signals were not due to a different magnitude of cytosolic Ca2+ elevations.
source: The compartmental differences in mitochondrial signals were not due to a different magnitude of cytosolic Ca2+ elevations.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing similar cytosolic Ca2+ levels across compartments despite different mitochondrial responses.

claim: The peak ΔF/F amplitude of Fura-2 transients elicited by twenty spikes was 26% ± 3.6% (n = 22) for soma, 37% ± 4% (n = 13) for apical dendrite, 38% ± 4% (n = 13) for basal dendrites, and 25% ± 4% in the AIS (n = 7).
source: For example, the peak ΔF/F amplitude of Fura-2 transients elicited by twenty spikes was 26% ± 3.6% (n = 22) for soma, 37% ± 4% (n = 13) for apical dendrite, 38% ± 4% (n = 13) for basal dendrites, and 25% ± 4% in the AIS (n = 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data on cytosolic Ca2+ responses.

claim: The compartmental differences in magnitude of the mitoGCaMP6m transients could not be explained by lower expression level of fluorescence probe in the mitochondria localized within the thinner neuronal processes.
source: The compartmental differences in magnitude of the mitoGCaMP6m transients could, at least partially, be explained by the lower expression level of fluorescence probe in the mitochondria localized within the thinner neuronal processes. This seems to be unlikely, however, since, in all neuronal compartments, maximal mitoGCaMP6m fluorescence of the individual mitochondria following prolonged depolarization of the neuronal membrane was similar (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: There exists an as-yet-unidentified mechanism that differentially regulates the mitochondrial Ca2+ entry in distinct neuronal compartments.
source: Our evidence, therefore, points to the existence of an as-yet-unidentified mechanism that differentially regulates the mitochondrial Ca2+ entry in distinct neuronal compartments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that compartmental differences in mitochondrial Ca2+ responses cannot be explained by probe expression or cytosolic Ca2+ levels.

claim: As spike frequency increased, the rise of cytosolic Ca2+ transients became progressively faster and their peak amplitude modestly increased.
source: As spike frequency increased, the rise of cytosolic Ca2+ transients became progressively faster and their peak amplitude modestly increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mitochondrial Ca2+ signals showed a very different frequency dependence than cytosolic Ca2+ signals.
source: In contrast, the mitochondrial Ca2+ signals showed a very different frequency dependence.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing frequency dependence of cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ signals.

claim: Firing at a frequency of 20 Hz or lower elicited a minimal elevation in [Ca2+]m, whereas the response to spikes at a frequency of 50 Hz or higher was dramatically greater.
source: Firing at a frequency of 20 Hz or lower elicited a minimal elevation in [Ca2+]m, whereas the response to spikes at a frequency of 50 Hz or higher was dramatically greater.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The steep frequency dependence of the mitochondrial signals was observed in all neuronal compartments, including somas, apical, and basal dendrites.
source: The steep frequency dependence of the mitochondrial signals was observed in all neuronal compartments, including somas, apical, and basal dendrites, making it unlikely that it reflects the frequency-dependent failure of AP backpropagation (Spruston et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations across different neuronal compartments.

claim: The frequency-dependent amplification of mitochondrial Ca2+ transients does not reflect the frequency-dependent failure of AP backpropagation.
source: The steep frequency dependence of the mitochondrial signals was observed in all neuronal compartments, including somas, apical, and basal dendrites, making it unlikely that it reflects the frequency-dependent failure of AP backpropagation (Spruston et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that frequency dependence occurs in all compartments, not just dendrites where backpropagation failure would be expected.

claim: The frequency-dependent amplification of mitochondrial Ca2+ transients was observed in all 21 neurons tested with either 50, 20, or 5 APs.
source: The frequency-dependent amplification of mitochondrial Ca2+ transients was observed in all 21 neurons tested with either 50, 20, or 5 APs (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 21 neurons shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The mean ratio of peak amplitudes of the mitochondrial Ca2+ transients elicited by trains of spikes at 50 and 20 Hz was larger when neurons were subjected to longer (3.36 ± 0.46 times, n = 22 for 50 APs) than to shorter (1.74 ± 0.18 times, n = 5 for 5 APs) trains.
source: The mean ratio of peak amplitudes of the mitochondrial Ca2+ transients elicited by trains of spikes at 50 and 20 Hz was larger when neurons were subjected to longer (3.36 ± 0.46 times, n = 22 for 50 APs) than to shorter (1.74 ± 0.18 times, n = 5 for 5 APs) trains (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The peak amplitude of mito-Ca2+ transients behaved as Bolzmannian function of the frequency, with mean half-amplitude of 38 Hz and steepness of 22 Hz–1 (n = 12).
source: Systematic varying of AP frequency in a range from 10 to 100 Hz revealed that the peak amplitude of mito-Ca2+ transients behaved as Bolzmannian function of the frequency, with mean half-amplitude of 38 Hz and steepness of 22 Hz–1 (n = 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of frequency-response relationship from 12 neurons.

claim: The decay time course of the mitochondrial Ca2+ transients elicited by high-frequency spike trains was significantly slower than those produced by the same number of spikes at a lower frequency.
source: The decay time course of the mitochondrial Ca2+ transients elicited by high-frequency spike trains was significantly slower than those produced by the same number of spikes at a lower frequency (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Trains of fifty APs at 50 Hz elicited the extremely slowly decaying mito-Ca2+ transients (τ > 10 s) in 11/15 somas and 7/10 apical dendrites.
source: Thus, trains of fifty APs at 50 Hz elicited the extremely slowly decaying mito-Ca2+ transients (τ > 10 s) in 11/15 somas and 7/10 apical dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data on decay kinetics.

claim: All but one mito-Ca2+ transient produced in the same neurons by fifty APs at 20 Hz decayed rapidly.
source: In contrast, all but one mito-Ca2+ transient produced in the same neurons by fifty APs at 20 Hz decayed rapidly.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing decay kinetics at different frequencies.

claim: In cortical neurons, NAD(P)H signals primarily reflect changes in mitochondrial NAD(P)H pool.
source: In cortical neurons, NAD(P)H signals primarily reflect changes in mitochondrial NAD(P)H pool (Díaz-García et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research on NAD(P)H signals.

claim: In response to electrical stimulation, a negative deflection in the NAD(P)H autofluorescence ('dip') indicates an increased rate of electron transfer reflected in NAD(P)H oxidation.
source: In response to electrical stimulation, we observed a negative deflection in the NAD(P)H autofluorescence ('dip') which indicates an increased rate of electron transfer reflected in NAD(P)H oxidation, followed by a positive transient ('overshoot') which indicates Krebs-cycle-dependent replenishment of NAD(P)H pool.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about NAD(P)H fluorescence changes and experimental observations.

claim: A positive transient ('overshoot') in NAD(P)H autofluorescence indicates Krebs-cycle-dependent replenishment of NAD(P)H pool.
source: In response to electrical stimulation, we observed a negative deflection in the NAD(P)H autofluorescence ('dip') which indicates an increased rate of electron transfer reflected in NAD(P)H oxidation, followed by a positive transient ('overshoot') which indicates Krebs-cycle-dependent replenishment of NAD(P)H pool.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about NAD(P)H fluorescence changes and experimental observations.

claim: At higher stimulation frequency, the magnitude of both dip and overshoot of the NAD(P)H signals were enhanced.
source: At higher stimulation frequency, the magnitude of both dip and overshoot of the NAD(P)H signals were enhanced, consistent with the previous reports that the rates of NAD(P)H oxidation and synthesis are dependent on the Ca2+ level in the mitochondrial matrix (Díaz-García et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and is consistent with previous research.

claim: The rates of NAD(P)H oxidation and synthesis are dependent on the Ca2+ level in the mitochondrial matrix.
source: At higher stimulation frequency, the magnitude of both dip and overshoot of the NAD(P)H signals were enhanced, consistent with the previous reports that the rates of NAD(P)H oxidation and synthesis are dependent on the Ca2+ level in the mitochondrial matrix (Díaz-García et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The changes in NAD(P)H fluorescence were spatially restricted to Layer 5 of a single cortical column.
source: Spatio-temporal analysis of the NAD(P)H autofluorescence dynamics at two stimulation frequencies (Figure 3b) revealed that the changes in the fluorescence were spatially restricted to Layer 5 of a single cortical column and that the frequency-dependent amplification of both dip and overshoot amplitude was relatively uniform within the stimulated region.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The frequency-dependent amplification of both dip and overshoot amplitude was relatively uniform within the stimulated region.
source: Spatio-temporal analysis of the NAD(P)H autofluorescence dynamics at two stimulation frequencies (Figure 3b) revealed that the changes in the fluorescence were spatially restricted to Layer 5 of a single cortical column and that the frequency-dependent amplification of both dip and overshoot amplitude was relatively uniform within the stimulated region.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The dip amplitude of NAD(P)H signals increased from –15 ± 2 a.u. at 20 Hz to –21 ± 2 a.u. at 50 Hz (n = 15 ROIs, p < 0.001).
source: The dip amplitude increased from –15 ± 2 a.u. at 20 Hz to –21 ± 2 a.u. at 50 Hz (n = 15 ROIs, p < 0.001), the overshoot's peak amplitude increased from 8 ± 2 a.u. to 19 ± 3 a.u. (p < 0.001) and the overshoot area increased from 156 ± 46 a.u.∙s to 441 ± 71 a.u.∙s (p < 0.001), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from 10 cortical slices.

claim: The overshoot's peak amplitude of NAD(P)H signals increased from 8 ± 2 a.u. to 19 ± 3 a.u. (p < 0.001) when stimulation frequency increased from 20 Hz to 50 Hz.
source: The dip amplitude increased from –15 ± 2 a.u. at 20 Hz to –21 ± 2 a.u. at 50 Hz (n = 15 ROIs, p < 0.001), the overshoot's peak amplitude increased from 8 ± 2 a.u. to 19 ± 3 a.u. (p < 0.001) and the overshoot area increased from 156 ± 46 a.u.∙s to 441 ± 71 a.u.∙s (p < 0.001), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data.

claim: The overshoot area of NAD(P)H signals increased from 156 ± 46 a.u.∙s to 441 ± 71 a.u.∙s (p < 0.001) when stimulation frequency increased from 20 Hz to 50 Hz.
source: The dip amplitude increased from –15 ± 2 a.u. at 20 Hz to –21 ± 2 a.u. at 50 Hz (n = 15 ROIs, p < 0.001), the overshoot's peak amplitude increased from 8 ± 2 a.u. to 19 ± 3 a.u. (p < 0.001) and the overshoot area increased from 156 ± 46 a.u.∙s to 441 ± 71 a.u.∙s (p < 0.001), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data.

claim: NAD(P)H signals in response to trains of stimuli delivered to the Stratum oriens in hippocampus were significantly enhanced at the higher stimulation frequency.
source: As in the neocortex, NAD(P)H signals in response to trains of stimuli delivered to the Stratum oriens were significantly enhanced at the higher stimulation frequency.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from hippocampal slices shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A single brief stimulus with its amplitude adjusted to keep the subsequent EPSP below the threshold for postsynaptic spike generation produced no detectable cytosolic or mitochondrial Ca2+ signals (n = 7).
source: Delivery of a single brief stimulus (0.1ms), with its amplitude adjusted to keep the subsequent EPSP below the threshold for postsynaptic spike generation produced no detectable cytosolic or mitochondrial Ca2+ signals (n = 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from 7 neurons.

claim: A single AP elicited by brief somatic current pulse injection produced a cytosolic but no mitochondrial Ca2+ response in the dendrites.
source: The single AP elicited by brief somatic current pulse injection, however, produced a cytosolic but no mitochondrial Ca2+ response in the dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The coincidence of the EPSP and backpropagating AP synergized to elicit a robust cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ response.
source: Remarkably, the coincidence of the EPSP and backpropagating AP synergized to elicit a robust cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ response (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: While most dendritic mitochondria were silent, the EPSP and AP coincidence created single localized mitochondrial Ca2+ 'hotspots' with peak ΔF/F amplitude of 6.4% ± 0.8% (n = 8) in the dendritic regions of interest.
source: While most dendritic mitochondria were silent, the EPSP and AP coincidence created single localized mitochondrial Ca2+ "hotspots" with peak ΔF/F amplitude of 6.4% ± 0.8% (n = 8) in the dendritic regions of interest.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data from 8 neurons.

claim: The appearance of mitochondrial Ca2+ hotspots provides evidence for a highly restricted, probably single mitochondrial Ca2+ elevation, in the vicinity of the active spine.
source: We interpreted the appearance of these hotspots as evidence for a highly restricted, probably single mitochondrial Ca2+ elevation, in the vicinity of the active spine.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of localized mitochondrial Ca2+ hotspots.

claim: The unitary character of the mitochondrial signals can be explained by a spatial sparseness of the synapses formed by the presynaptic fiber on the dendrites of the postsynaptic cortical cell.
source: The unitary character of the mitochondrial signals under this experimental paradigm can be explained by a spatial sparseness of the synapses formed by the presynaptic fiber on the dendrites of the postsynaptic cortical cell (Markram et al., 1997a) such that only one out of a few currently active spines could be found in the relatively short segment of a dendritic branch that we examined.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations and cited research on synaptic connectivity.

claim: The cytosolic Ca2+ elevation, measured in the same hotspot at which the mitoGCaMP6m signal was detected, was not significantly larger than in the nearby dendrite.
source: The cytosolic Ca2+ elevation, measured in the same hotspot at which the mitoGCaMP6m signal was detected, was not significantly larger than in the nearby dendrite.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: The failure to see the cytosolic Ca2+ 'hotspots' is most probably due to temporal and amplitude resolution of optical recording that was insufficient to reveal Ca2+ elevation in the tiny volume between the spine neck and the mitochondrion during the fast single spine Ca2+ transient.
source: The failure to see the cytosolic Ca2+ "hotspots" is, most probably, due to temporal and amplitude resolution of our optical recording that was insufficient to reveal Ca2+ elevation in the tiny volume between the spine neck and the mitochondrion during the fast single spine Ca2+ transient (Miyazaki and Ross, 2017; Svoboda et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is inferred from technical limitations and cited research on spine Ca2+ dynamics.

claim: In both apical and basal dendrites, the paired APs produced a significantly larger mitochondrial signal than unpaired APs.
source: In both apical and basal dendrites, the paired APs produced a significantly larger mitochondrial signal.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b-c.

claim: The cytosolic Ca2+ elevation amplitude was not significantly different for unpaired and paired stimulation.
source: In contrast, the cytosolic Ca2+ elevation amplitude was not significantly different for unpaired and paired stimulation (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b-c.

claim: The peak amplitude of the mitoGCaMP6m transients elicited by paired APs was 2.73 ± 0.32 (n = 8) times higher than of those evoked by the unpaired APs in the basal dendrites.
source: Hence, the peak amplitude of the mitoGCaMP6m transients elicited by paired APs was 2.73 ± 0.32 (n = 8) and 2.11 ± 0.32 (n = 9) times higher than of those evoked by the unpaired APs in the basal and apical dendrites, respectively (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The peak amplitude of the mitoGCaMP6m transients elicited by paired APs was 2.11 ± 0.32 (n = 9) times higher than of those evoked by the unpaired APs in the apical dendrites.
source: Hence, the peak amplitude of the mitoGCaMP6m transients elicited by paired APs was 2.73 ± 0.32 (n = 8) and 2.11 ± 0.32 (n = 9) times higher than of those evoked by the unpaired APs in the basal and apical dendrites, respectively (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The ability of postsynaptic neurons to generate an AP was crucial for triggering the dendritic mito-Ca2+ transients.
source: The ability of postsynaptic neurons to generate an AP was crucial for triggering the dendritic mito-Ca2+ transients.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using QX-314 to block postsynaptic APs, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intracellular dialysis with a solution containing QX-314, which prevented the firing of the postsynaptic cells, dramatically reduced the amplitude of synaptically evoked mito-Ca2+ transients.
source: Thus, intracellular dialysis with a solution containing a blocker of voltage-gated Na+ channels, QX-314, which prevented the firing of the postsynaptic cells (Connors and Prince, 1982) while producing only a minor effect on the EPSP generation, dramatically reduced the amplitude of synaptically evoked mito-Ca2+ transients (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Even the significantly larger EPSPs evoked in QX-314 dialyzed neurons by a train of strong synaptic stimuli, in the absence of AP, produced no significant Ca2+ elevation in dendritic mitochondria.
source: As with single subthreshold EPSPs, even the significantly larger EPSPs evoked in QX-314 dialyzed neurons by a train of strong synaptic stimuli, in the absence of AP, produced no significant Ca2+ elevation in dendritic mitochondria.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations with QX-314.

claim: The main route of Ca2+ entry into the spines is via the NMDARs.
source: It is well established that the main route of Ca2+ entry into the spines is via the NMDARs (Mainen et al., 1999; Miyazaki and Ross, 2017), which require glutamate and depolarization to relieve the Mg2+ block (Nowak et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on spine Ca2+ entry mechanisms.

claim: NMDARs require glutamate and depolarization to relieve the Mg2+ block.
source: It is well established that the main route of Ca2+ entry into the spines is via the NMDARs (Mainen et al., 1999; Miyazaki and Ross, 2017), which require glutamate and depolarization to relieve the Mg2+ block (Nowak et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research on NMDAR properties.

claim: Blockade of NMDARs by bath applied APV (50 µM) almost completely and reversibly abolished the mitoGCaMP6m transients evoked by the paired APs in the dendrites.
source: Blockade of NMDARs by bath applied APV (50 µM) almost completely and reversibly abolished the mitoGCaMP6m transients evoked by the paired APs in the dendrites (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a tight, causative relationship between neuronal electrical activity, cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ levels.
source: In contrast to a recent report of 'loose' coupling of mitochondrial Ca2+ transients to neuronal activity and cytosolic Ca2+ transients in in vivo cortical neurons (Lin et al., 2019), our data suggest a tight, causative relationship between neuronal electrical activity, cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and contrasts with previous reports.

claim: Several studies have revealed the tens-of-seconds long mitochondrial Ca2+ transients in presynaptic terminals of cultured central neurons.
source: Several studies (Ashrafi et al., 2020; Devaraju et al., 2017; Kwon et al., 2016; Lewis et al., 2018) have revealed the tens-of-seconds long mitochondrial Ca2+ transients in presynaptic terminals of cultured central neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The extremely slow rate of Ca2+ clearance in presynaptic terminals may be due to excessively intense stimulation rather than compartmental specialization.
source: While this extremely slow rate of Ca2+ clearance may reflect compartmental specialization of mitochondrial Ca2+ handling at the presynaptic sites, it seems more likely to be due to excessively intense stimulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison with other experimental results and represents speculation about the cause of slow clearance.

claim: Small mitochondrial Ca2+ signals in axons of cultured hippocampal neurons elicited by 1–5 antidromic stimuli decayed rapidly.
source: Indeed, small mitochondrial Ca2+ signals in axons of cultured hippocampal neurons elicited by 1–5 antidromic stimuli decayed rapidly (Gazit et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The prolonged mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations occur only following the long period of robust high-frequency firing.
source: Our results indicate that the prolonged mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations occur only following the long period of robust high-frequency firing.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on decay kinetics.

claim: Intense firing during various neurological diseases may contribute to the mitochondrial Ca2+ overload and disease progression.
source: Although such intense firing is not typically observed in cortical pyramidal cells under physiological conditions, it may occur during various neurological diseases (Makinson et al., 2017; Zott et al., 2019) contributing to the mitochondrial Ca2+ overload and disease progression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results and cited research on neurological diseases.

claim: The summation of the unitary AP-evoked mitochondrial Ca2+ transients steeply depends on firing frequency.
source: Our evidence indicates that the summation of the unitary AP-evoked mitochondrial Ca2+ transients steeply depends on firing frequency.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on frequency dependence.

claim: Cytosolic Ca2+ signaling is less sensitive to firing rate than mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling.
source: Thus, in contrast to cytosolic Ca2+ signaling, which is less sensitive to firing rate, the mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations were strongly amplified at firing frequencies of >40 Hz.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca2+ responses to different firing frequencies.

claim: Mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations were strongly amplified at firing frequencies of >40 Hz.
source: Thus, in contrast to cytosolic Ca2+ signaling, which is less sensitive to firing rate, the mitochondrial Ca2+ elevations were strongly amplified at firing frequencies of >40 Hz.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on frequency dependence.

claim: The enhanced mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake accelerated the rate of NAD(P)H production and consumption via the tricarboxylic acid cycle and the electron transport chain, thereby upregulating the ATP synthesis.
source: As expected, the enhanced mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake accelerated the rate of NAD(P)H production and consumption via the tricarboxylic acid cycle and the electron transport chain, respectively (Díaz-García et al., 2021), thereby upregulating the ATP synthesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on NAD(P)H dynamics and cited research.

claim: Action potential induced mitochondrial Ca2+ transients are about threefold greater in the soma and apical dendrites than in proximal axon and basal dendrites.
source: The finding that action potential induced mitochondrial Ca2+ transients are about threefold greater in the soma and apical dendrites than in proximal axon and basal dendrites, most likely, indicates the compartmental difference in expression of mitochondrial Ca2+ channel, MCU.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on compartmental differences.

claim: The compartmental differences in mitochondrial Ca2+ transients most likely indicate the compartmental difference in expression of mitochondrial Ca2+ channel, MCU.
source: The finding that action potential induced mitochondrial Ca2+ transients are about threefold greater in the soma and apical dendrites than in proximal axon and basal dendrites, most likely, indicates the compartmental difference in expression of mitochondrial Ca2+ channel, MCU.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental observations of compartmental differences.

claim: The subcellular differences in mitochondrial Ca2+ handling may reflect region-specific MCU molecular tuning or mitochondrial morphology.
source: Alternatively, the subcellular differences in mitochondrial Ca2+ handling may reflect region-specific MCU molecular tuning (Ashrafi et al., 2020; Patron et al., 2019) or mitochondrial morphology (Lewis et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on cited research on potential mechanisms.

claim: The greater mitochondrial Ca2+ transients in thick neuronal processes might be necessary to compensate for the higher energetic cost of AP generation.
source: From the functional viewpoint, the greater mitochondrial Ca2+ transients in thick neuronal processes might be necessary to compensate for the higher energetic cost of AP generation (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001).
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from functional considerations and cited research.

claim: The metabolic activity of mitochondria plays a pivotal role in synaptic plasticity.
source: A recent study suggests that the metabolic activity of mitochondria plays a pivotal role in synaptic plasticity (Rangaraju et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Mitochondria can detect the Hebbian time coincidences between the pre- and postsynaptic spikes.
source: Our results suggest that mitochondria can detect the Hebbian time coincidences between the pre- and postsynaptic spikes (Markram et al., 1997b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on spike-timing-dependent mitochondrial responses.

claim: The resultant Ca2+ elevations in the mitochondrial matrix could be an essential part of the cascade of events underlying spike-time-dependent synaptic plasticity.
source: The resultant Ca2+ elevations in the mitochondrial matrix could be an essential part of the cascade of events underlying spike-time-dependent synaptic plasticity.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental results.

claim: The cascade of events underlying STDP might involve the initiation of fission of the dendritic mitochondria.
source: This cascade might involve the initiation of fission of the dendritic mitochondria, as has been proposed for chemically induced NMDAR-dependent LTP in hippocampal neuronal culture (Divakaruni et al., 2018), although it remains unclear whether the LTP associated burst of fission events occurs at a physiologically relevant time scale.
evidence: The claim is speculative and based on cited research, with caveats about physiological relevance.

claim: The involvement of the frequency-dependent mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling explains the observed repetition rate requirement for LTP induction.
source: The involvement of the frequency-dependent mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling, most probably, explains the observed repetition rate requirement for LTP induction (Inglebert et al., 2020; Lisman and Spruston, 2005; Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results and cited research on LTP induction requirements.

claim: Spike-timing-dependent potentiation of cortical synapses, in addition to precise spike timing, requires a sufficiently high repetition frequency.
source: Indeed, the spike-timing-dependent potentiation of cortical synapses, in addition to precise spike timing, requires a sufficiently high repetition frequency (Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The unique ability of the mitochondria to decode firing frequency and Hebbian timing code of neuronal activity make this organelle a long-thought link between the firing pattern, metabolism, and plasticity.
source: Our data indicate that the unique ability of the mitochondria to decode firing frequency and Hebbian timing code of neuronal activity make this organelle a long-thought link between the firing pattern, metabolism, and plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing frequency and timing dependence of mitochondrial responses.
